data.title: Glycolic acid (cream, lotion, peel)
data.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · α-hydroxy acid (AHA) — smallest AHA (from sugar cane)
data.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** α-hydroxy acid (AHA) — smallest AHA (from sugar cane)

## Mechanism of action
- Reduces corneocyte cohesion (loosens the stratum corneum) → exfoliation
- At higher concentrations: dermal effects — increases collagen and glycosaminoglycan production
- Disperses melanin and speeds removal of pigmented keratinocytes

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Creams/lotions 6–12% (home use): xerosis, ichthyosis, keratosis pilaris, photoageing, acne (comedonal), melasma and PIH (adjunct), dull skin
- Chemical peels 20–70% (superficial peels, office use): acne, melasma, PIH, photoageing, superficial scars
- Also in the anti-acne list (glycolic acid cream)

## Dose & formulations
- Creams: once daily at night, starting with lower strength; sunscreen during the day
- Peels: start 20–35% for 2–3 min, increase strength and time every 2–4 weeks; neutralise with sodium bicarbonate solution or water

## Adverse effects
- Stinging, redness, dryness, peeling
- Photosensitivity — use sunscreen
- Peels: frosting/burns if left too long, PIH (dark skin), herpes reactivation

## Contraindications
- Active infection, open wounds, inflamed eczema/rosacea; recent isotretinoin (peels — relative)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Low-strength creams and superficial peels are considered safe.

## Viva points
- Smallest AHA — penetrates best
- Glycolic acid peels are time-dependent — must be neutralised
- Increases sun sensitivity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.52 (α-Hydroxy acids) and ch.53 (Chemical peels); Khopkar ch.31. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
